edition.title: P100 NEWS + CULTURE + SPORT + SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY
edition.deck: A Republican defeat fuels open dissent over the Iran war, while Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong receives a 10-year sentence. Also: an Ebola evacuation to the UK and a new pause on a Danish data-centre project.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises consequential overnight developments and fresh reporting. Repeated coverage of the US election is grouped around the new public criticism by JD Vance; older stories without a substantial new development are not carried forward.

content.headline: Vance blames Iran war for Republican defeat in public break with Trump
content.shortHeadline: Vance blames Iran war for Republican defeat
content.standfirst: The vice-president says the conflict was the reason Republicans lost the midterms, sharpening questions about party loyalty and the 2028 race. Trump has also acknowledged the war played a part in the result, but says he would launch it again.

image.caption: JD Vance at an event in Hendersonville, North Carolina.

sources.originalTitle: Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war
JD Vance says US war on Iran is ‘real reason’ Republicans lost midterm elections
Republikanerne peger fingre og taler om en 'genstart' efter midtvejsvalget

segments.body: JD Vance said the Iran war was the reason Republicans lost the midterms, in a lengthy post on X published after Democrats took control of both chambers of Congress. He argued the party must face the cost of the conflict and listed ending the war and tackling living costs among its priorities.

segments.title: A party looking ahead
segments.body: Vance did not name Trump in his post, and the BBC reports he showed the statement to the president before publishing it. Trump said he knew Vance’s views and agreed the war had affected the result, while insisting the decision was right. Vance has not announced whether he will run for president in 2028.

DR reports that criticism of Trump is also coming from other Republicans, including former governor Mitt Romney and Senator Ted Cruz. But the party’s future direction remains uncertain, and Trump retains a loyal base of supporters.

perspectives.body: DR’s reporting points to a wider debate about whether Republicans will change course after the defeat, while cautioning that criticism from party figures does not mean Trump has lost the support of his core voters.

content.headline: Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years under security law
content.shortHeadline: Joshua Wong gets 10 years under Hong Kong security law
content.standfirst: The pro-democracy campaigner, already imprisoned for nearly six years, received a 10-year term after pleading guilty to colluding with foreign forces. Critics say the law is being used to punish dissent.

image.caption: Joshua Wong speaks to reporters in Hong Kong in 2019.

sources.originalTitle: Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in prison in national security case
Joshua Wong, face of Hong Kong's pro-democracy protests, jailed for 10 years
Demokratiforkæmper i Hongkong idømmes ti års fængsel

segments.body: Joshua Wong, 30, has been sentenced to 10 years in prison for colluding with foreign forces under Hong Kong’s national security law. He pleaded guilty in September. Prosecutors said he and other activists sought foreign sanctions and other measures against China and Hong Kong.

segments.title: Sentence and reaction
segments.body: Wong has been detained for nearly six years and was due to be released in January 2027 on an earlier sentence. The Guardian reports that two months of the new term will run concurrently with his remaining sentence. Nathan Law and human rights groups condemned the ruling, saying the law is being used to silence political opposition.

perspectives.body: Nathan Law called the sentence punishment for peaceful advocacy. Amnesty International said it was another example of the security law being used to punish dissent rather than protect national security.

content.headline: Ukraine says video shows second Russian strike killing people at shelter
content.shortHeadline: Ukraine says second strike hit village shelter
content.standfirst: Ukraine says at least 40 people died in Monday’s attack on a village aid centre and shelter, and more than 30 may remain under rubble. Russia has not publicly commented on the claims.

image.caption: Ukraine-released body-camera footage shows residents entering a shelter before a second blast.

sources.originalTitle: Ukraine says bodycam video shows deadly Russian double-tap bombing

segments.body: Ukraine’s police released body-camera footage that they say shows residents entering an underground shelter after an initial bomb strike in Kamyshuvakha, followed seconds later by another blast. Kyiv says at least 40 people were killed and more than 30 may still be under the rubble as the search continues.

segments.title: Claims and diplomacy
segments.body: Ukraine says nine aerial bombs struck the village as people gathered to receive aid, and accuses Russia of hitting rescuers and police as well. BBC Verify confirmed the footage was filmed at the same location as other images of the aftermath. The Russian military has not publicly commented. Separately, Kyiv says talks with US envoys and other officials are under way ahead of planned trilateral negotiations in Abu Dhabi.

content.headline: Hackers transfer about €100m from French bank in cyberattack
content.shortHeadline: French bank reports cyberattack involving €100m
content.standfirst: Crédit Mutuel Arkéa says hackers accessed the bank’s own account and made transfers to other banks; customers’ accounts were not accessed. French prosecutors have opened an investigation, but the bank has not disclosed its losses or who was responsible.

sources.originalTitle: Fransk bank melder om cyberangreb med overførsler for millioner

segments.body: French regional bank Crédit Mutuel Arkéa says hackers accessed its own account and made fraudulent transfers worth about €100m. The bank says customers’ accounts were not reached and customers suffered no financial loss. Some transfers were blocked, and efforts to recover funds are under way.

segments.title: Investigation continues
segments.body: The bank described the incident as a sophisticated external attack and rejected the possibility of human error, but has not explained how it happened or identified those responsible. Paris prosecutors have opened an investigation. The amount ultimately lost is still being assessed, and the bank says the incident does not threaten its financial stability.

content.headline: Former US contractor admits passing classified intelligence to Ethiopia
content.shortHeadline: US contractor pleads guilty to sharing secrets with Ethiopia
content.standfirst: Abraham Teklu Lemma admitted sending classified material to senior Ethiopian officials, including intelligence he hoped would help target Tigrayan fighters. Prosecutors say Ethiopian officials used information he supplied in military operations.

image.caption: The two-year civil war in Ethiopia killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.

sources.originalTitle: US contractor gave Ethiopia secrets to help kill Tigray fighters

segments.body: Abraham Teklu Lemma, a former US government contractor, has pleaded guilty to conspiring to transmit national defence information to Ethiopia. Prosecutors say he removed classified material from secure facilities and shared it with senior Ethiopian political, military and intelligence figures between 2021 and his arrest in 2023.

segments.title: Links to the civil war
segments.body: The US Department of Justice says the material included satellite imagery and information about military activity. Prosecutors say Lemma hoped it would help Ethiopia identify and kill Tigrayan fighters; the FBI said Ethiopian officials later used intelligence he supplied in military operations. His sentencing is scheduled for 14 April 2027, and he faces up to 22 years under the plea agreement.

content.headline: El Niño fuels an unusually severe typhoon season across East Asia
content.shortHeadline: East Asia faces an unusually intense typhoon season
content.standfirst: A run of powerful storms has killed dozens and damaged crops and infrastructure across the region. Forecasters warn the season may not be over, while scientists say warmer Pacific waters are intensifying the risks.

image.caption: Fishermen return to sea after a typhoon hit China’s Jiangsu province.

sources.originalTitle: Typhoons batter East Asia as El Niño makes Pacific 'burn with fever'

segments.body: East Asia has faced a series of destructive storms in recent months, with typhoons disrupting flights and power, flooding communities and damaging crops. The report links the unusually intense season to El Niño, which has warmed Pacific waters and helped storms strengthen while travelling over warm seas.

segments.title: Preparing for further risk
segments.body: The report says the season may continue beyond its usual peak, with sea-surface temperatures in a monitored part of the equatorial Pacific reaching a record in October. Countries are taking steps including public warnings, improved monitoring and support for farmers, but the longer-term effect on communities will depend on decisions about infrastructure, water management and social protection.

content.headline: Mother and daughter found dead after suspected bear attack in Canada
content.shortHeadline: Mother and daughter die in suspected bear attack
content.standfirst: The women’s remains were found near Bella Coola, British Columbia, after they went missing during a walk. Authorities say evidence suggests an animal may have been involved, but it is not yet clear whether one or more bears were involved.

image.caption: Grizzly bears in British Columbia; file image.

sources.originalTitle: Mother and daughter die after suspected grizzly bear attack in Canada

segments.body: Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, were found dead in a trail area near Bella Coola after being reported missing on 1 November. British Columbia conservation officers said evidence at the scene suggested an animal may have been involved and are trying to locate any bears involved.

Authorities say it is not yet clear whether more than one bear may have been involved. Any captured bear would be assessed, and an animal found to have taken part in the attack would be killed under provincial safety guidelines. The family described the women as close and said they shared many hobbies.

content.headline: Cyberattack shuts fanfiction archive holding more than 18 million works
content.shortHeadline: Fanfiction archive with 18 million works shut after cyberattack
content.standfirst: Archive of Our Own says it will be offline for two to four weeks after a security incident. The site’s operators have not said whether its vast collection of fan-created stories has been lost.

sources.originalTitle: 18 millioner historier er forsvundet fra nettet – og fans frygter det værste

segments.body: Archive of Our Own, one of the world’s largest fanfiction websites, has closed following what it described as a security incident. DR reports that the site expects to remain offline for two to four weeks; it hosts more than 18 million works contributed by fans.

segments.title: What remains unknown
segments.body: The outage has prompted concern that stories and other archive material may be lost, but the reporting does not establish that any content has been deleted. The site has previously suffered a cyberattack: in 2023, a group calling itself Anonymous Sudan claimed responsibility for an attack that kept it offline for 28 days.

content.headline: British healthcare worker with Ebola to be evacuated from DR Congo
content.shortHeadline: British Ebola patient to be evacuated from DR Congo
content.standfirst: The patient is reported to be in a stable condition and will be taken to a specialist infectious-disease unit. The government says the risk to the wider UK public remains low.

image.caption: A humanitarian worker supports the response to the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo.

sources.originalTitle: British healthcare worker with Ebola evacuated from DR Congo to UK
British man infected with Ebola in DR Congo to be flown back to UK

segments.body: A British healthcare worker who tested positive for Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is being evacuated to the UK for treatment. The government says procedures for cases of this kind have been activated and that the risk to the public remains low.

segments.title: Outbreak context
segments.body: The worker is reported to be in a stable condition and is expected to be transferred to a specialist high-consequence infectious-disease unit. The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus and has recorded more than 10,000 cases and 5,000 deaths, according to the supplied reporting. There is no approved treatment for this variant; vaccine trials are under way.

content.headline: UK and Caribbean plan talks on slavery’s legacy, with reparations unresolved
content.shortHeadline: UK and Caribbean to begin talks on slavery’s legacy
content.standfirst: Commonwealth leaders say structured dialogue is expected within a year, but the UK has ruled out reparations. Caribbean campaigners say debt relief and development aid cannot substitute for reparatory justice.

image.caption: Gaston Browne met UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the Commonwealth summit.

sources.originalTitle: UK and Caribbean to begin ‘dialogue’ within next year after slavery reparations call

segments.body: The UK and Caribbean nations are expected to begin structured talks on slavery’s legacy within the next 12 months, according to Gaston Browne, prime minister of Antigua and Barbuda. He said leaders had agreed in principle to establish a framework by the end of this year or early next year.

segments.title: What the talks will cover
segments.body: The UK has proposed discussions on debt resets and announced £40m for Caribbean infrastructure over three years, while ruling out reparations. The Caribbean Community’s plan calls for debt cancellation and monetary compensation. Regional campaigners say development assistance cannot replace reparatory justice, and that affected communities must help decide what it involves.

perspectives.body: Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines, argues that the dialogue must address reparations specifically, rather than treating them as interchangeable with general development goals.

content.headline: Experts warn connected appliances could be vulnerable after refrigeration hacks
content.shortHeadline: Refrigeration hacks prompt warnings about connected devices
content.standfirst: Recent attacks on commercial refrigeration systems have renewed concern about internet-connected appliances and critical infrastructure. Experts say the UK household risk is lower, and the identity of the attackers has not been established.

image.caption: Internet-connected household appliances can carry security risks, experts say.

sources.originalTitle: If you have a ‘smart fridge’, you need to know these risks

segments.body: Hackers targeted remote-control systems for commercial refrigeration in several countries, following an earlier attack on French freezers, according to the i Paper. The incidents affected businesses, including some in Britain, but no attribution has been established; experts cited by the paper say a state actor such as Russia may be responsible.

segments.title: Household risk and safeguards
segments.body: Experts told the i Paper that domestic smart fridges are not thought to be at risk from the specific attacks on commercial control units, and that mass attacks on household devices are less likely. They nevertheless warn that connected appliances and components can be vulnerable. A cyber-security expert advises asking whether every household device needs to be connected to a network.

content.headline: HMRC bank-account debt recovery plan raises questions over safeguards
content.shortHeadline: HMRC debt plan prompts concern over bank-account safeguards
content.standfirst: From 2029, HMRC could order regular deductions from current accounts to recover some unpaid tax debts. Tax experts warn that the plan has no guaranteed minimum balance and could affect joint-account holders who do not owe the debt.

image.caption: Chancellor John Healey, who announced the proposed HMRC debt-recovery powers.

sources.originalTitle: How HMRC can now raid your bank account – and what you need to know

segments.body: The government plans to give HMRC powers to recover certain unpaid tax debts directly from bank accounts from July 2029. The proposed maximum is £5,000 for individuals and £10,000 for companies. People would receive 28 days’ notice and be offered an affordability assessment and a right to appeal.

segments.title: Concerns about the impact
segments.body: The proposal does not guarantee that a minimum amount will remain in an account, prompting concern that people could be left short of money for essential bills. HMRC could also seek payment from a joint account if no suitable sole account is available, even though the other account holder may not owe the tax. The government says affordability checks and other safeguards will apply.

perspectives.body: The Low Incomes Tax Reform Group says it is unclear how HMRC will decide whether someone can afford deductions, and warns that difficulties engaging with the department may reflect financial hardship or trouble understanding a tax request, rather than refusal to pay.

content.headline: Nine men deny offences in trial over alleged long-running sexual abuse
content.shortHeadline: Nine men deny offences in trial over alleged sexual abuse
content.standfirst: A court heard that investigators found more than a million images and videos on a phone belonging to a man who has admitted offences against his wife. Nine other men deny charges; the trial is expected to last at least six weeks.

sources.originalTitle: The nine men accused of sex offences against woman drugged and raped by her husband

segments.body: Nine men deny offences including rape and conspiracy to rape in a trial at Manchester’s Minshull Street Crown Court. Prosecutors say the case began after journalists uncovered an online group in which a man discussed abusing his wife while she was asleep or unconscious.

segments.title: Evidence heard in court
segments.body: The husband, who cannot be named to protect his wife’s anonymity, has pleaded guilty to 62 offences against her. Prosecutors told the court that his phone contained more than a million images and videos. The jury must decide whether the woman shown in the material was unconscious or pretending; the prosecution says she was unconscious. The other defendants deny the charges.

content.headline: Denmark’s tax talks: is Dansk Folkeparti a partner or leverage?
content.shortHeadline: Is Dansk Folkeparti a real player in Denmark’s tax talks?
content.standfirst: The government has brought Dansk Folkeparti into negotiations, but the party’s call for cheaper fuel differs from the tax cuts sought by other right-wing parties. Analysts say the move could be a way to pressure those parties; the outcome is unclear.

image.caption: The tax negotiations raise questions about Dansk Folkeparti’s role.

sources.originalTitle: Magtens Morgenbrief: Er Messerschmidt regeringens lokkedue?

segments.body: The government’s tax negotiations have taken an unexpected turn with Dansk Folkeparti joining the talks. The party is demanding cheaper petrol and diesel for at least a year, while four other right-wing parties have sought tax cuts for lower earners and an end to a proposed tax measure.

segments.title: Negotiating tactic or deal?
segments.body: Political commentators quoted by DR say the government may be keeping multiple options open and using divisions among the right-wing parties to secure its tax agreement on favourable terms. One former adviser says Dansk Folkeparti risks being tied to the government’s economic policy if it compromises. Talks with the other right-wing parties are due to continue Thursday.

content.headline: Tårnby pauses proposed data-centre project after residents’ concerns
content.shortHeadline: Tårnby pauses data-centre plans after residents’ concerns
content.standfirst: The mayor announced a pause after about 300 people attended a public meeting. The municipality says it will consider residents’ concerns and await the government’s national data-centre strategy.

image.caption: Residents gather at Tårnby town hall for a meeting about the proposed data centre.

sources.originalTitle: Naboer er bekymrede for datacenter: Nu sætter kommunen projektet i bero

segments.body: Tårnby municipality has paused the construction process for a planned data centre on Ugandavej, where it sold 40,000 square metres of land for the project. Mayor Allan S. Andersen announced the pause at a public meeting attended by about 300 people.

Residents voiced opposition and asked for more involvement. The mayor acknowledged that the municipality had not been good enough at addressing concerns when the plan was first advanced two years ago. Tårnby also plans to wait for the national strategy on data centres, which the government has said will come before the end of the year.

content.headline: Danish business leaders temper relief at US midterm result
content.shortHeadline: Danish business sees both relief and risks after US vote
content.standfirst: A clear result and Trump’s acceptance of it eased some uncertainty for Danish companies, but the president remains in office and can still affect trade. Democratic control of Congress may also limit business-friendly measures.

sources.originalTitle: ANALYSE Danske topdirektører knus-elsker ikke den blå bølge i USA

segments.body: Danish business leaders are cautiously relieved that the US midterm result was clear and Donald Trump accepted it, DR reports. But the president remains in office, and his policies can still affect Danish companies through trade, energy and pharmaceutical markets.

segments.title: Exposure to US policy
segments.body: DR’s analysis points to the importance of the US market for Danish companies, including Novo Nordisk and exporters affected by shifting tariffs. It says Democratic control of Congress may constrain further business-friendly measures, though the scope for change and its effect on companies remain uncertain.

content.headline: Conductor Herbert Blomstedt dies aged 99 after a 71-year career
content.shortHeadline: Conductor Herbert Blomstedt dies aged 99
content.standfirst: The Swedish conductor had a decades-long relationship with DR Symphony Orchestra, which he first led in 1955. His final concert was in San Francisco earlier this year.

image.caption: Herbert Blomstedt rehearses with DR Symphony Orchestra.

sources.originalTitle: Verdens ældste dirigent var et 'mirakel'. Nu er han død

segments.body: Herbert Blomstedt, described by his agency as the world’s oldest conductor, has died at his home in Gothenburg aged 99. He had hoped to continue conducting until he was 100, but the agency said increasing health problems had forced him to cancel recent engagements.

segments.title: A long connection with Denmark
segments.body: Blomstedt first conducted DR Symphony Orchestra in 1955 and was its chief conductor from 1967 to 1977. He remained a regular guest and was named honorary conductor. His last concert was in San Francisco in May; he had been due to conduct two concerts at DR Koncerthuset next year.

content.headline: Liverpool lose 3-2 at Fenerbahce after twice taking the lead
content.shortHeadline: Liverpool surrender lead in 3-2 loss at Fenerbahce
content.standfirst: Liverpool’s first Champions League defeat by Fenerbahce came after they led twice, including through Alexander Isak’s 69th-minute header. Andoni Iraola called the goals conceded “cheap” and “messy”.

image.caption: Liverpool suffered their first Champions League defeat by Fenerbahce.

sources.originalTitle: Another 'miracle' in Istanbul - but this one hurt Liverpool

segments.body: Liverpool were beaten 3-2 in Istanbul after taking the lead twice. Trey Nyoni opened the scoring, and Alexander Isak put them ahead again in the 69th minute, but Fenerbahce struck three times from set-pieces to complete the comeback.

segments.title: A familiar defensive concern
segments.body: Former Liverpool defender Stephen Warnock said the defeat exposed recurring problems: mistakes at set-pieces and balls into the box, and a team that can look vulnerable on the counter-attack. He said Liverpool’s inability to see out a game after going ahead was frustrating for supporters.

content.headline: LIV Golf set to wind down after replacement funding falls through
content.shortHeadline: LIV Golf faces wind-down as replacement funding falls through
content.standfirst: The financing firm that had considered backing a new version of LIV Golf has decided a deal is not viable. An attorney is expected to tell a court on Thursday that the LIV 2.0 proposal cannot proceed.

sources.originalTitle: LIV to wind down after backers withdraw support

segments.body: LIV Golf is set to be wound down after BC Partners Credit withdrew from a possible financing deal, BBC Sport reports. The firm had considered providing about $300m for LIV 2.0, after Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund withdrew its backing in April.

segments.title: A proposed revival stalled
segments.body: Sources told BBC Sport that the LIV 2.0 team had commitments from co-investors and about 30 players, including major winners, but could not secure the agreements needed in time. The expected court announcement would mark a major turn in a saga that has unsettled the golf calendar and left players’ futures uncertain.

content.headline: Tenerife mourns De Miguel as goalkeeper Owono speaks of his grief
content.shortHeadline: Tenerife mourns De Miguel; Owono speaks of his grief
content.standfirst: Tributes have gathered at Tenerife’s stadium after striker Jesus de Miguel died from injuries sustained in a collision during Monday’s match. FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono says he is struggling to come to terms with the loss.

image.caption: Fans gather to pay their respects to Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel.

sources.originalTitle: An island in mourning: Tenerife processes death of De Miguel
'Most difficult days of my life' for keeper Owono

segments.body: Fans have laid flowers, scarves, photographs and children’s drawings outside Tenerife’s stadium, where hundreds have gathered to pay their respects. De Miguel, 30, died after a collision with Owono during a match on Monday. Tenerife said six official days of mourning would begin.

segments.title: Owono’s statement
segments.body: Owono said through his club that these were “the most difficult days of my life” and that he could think only of De Miguel and the pain felt by those who loved him. Police have opened a routine investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter; the inquiry is ongoing.

perspectives.body: Owono said he would face whatever issues arose with respect, but that his thoughts were with De Miguel, his family and everyone who loved him. His club also said team-mate Lautaro Spatz described the goalkeeper as devastated and said he would never intentionally hurt anyone.

content.headline: Djokovic’s ATP Finals hopes end as Zverev questions scrutiny of his ranking
content.shortHeadline: Djokovic out of ATP Finals race; Zverev questions scrutiny
content.standfirst: Novak Djokovic lost to qualifier Rinky Hijikata in Paris and can no longer qualify for the ATP Finals. Alexander Zverev, also beaten at the Masters, said he was annoyed at having to justify becoming world number one.

sources.originalTitle: Defeat ends Djokovic's hopes of making ATP Finals
Zverev annoyed by reaction to becoming world number one

segments.body: Djokovic’s 2-6 6-3 6-3 defeat by world number 83 Hijikata ended his bid to reach the ATP Finals in Turin. He was likely to need a semi-final run in Paris to qualify. Djokovic said his plan for the coming weeks was “just rest” after a season in which he failed to reach the quarter-finals at any Masters 1000 event.

segments.title: Zverev objects to the reaction
segments.body: Zverev lost his first match since becoming world number one, going down 7-6 (7-5) 6-2 to Lorenzo Musetti. He said it was “annoying” that he felt he had to explain why it was acceptable for him to hold the ranking, while acknowledging he had played badly against Musetti.

content.headline: Brazilian under-20 match sees record 51 red cards after brawl
content.shortHeadline: Record 51 red cards shown after Brazilian youth-game brawl
content.standfirst: The abandoned Minas Gerais Under-20 Championship semi-final between Uberlandia and Mamore produced 51 dismissals: 43 players and eight members of staff. Uberlandia later conceded the second leg, saying Mamore had only seven players available.

image.caption: Players and staff were sent off after a brawl during the under-20 match.

sources.originalTitle: World record 51 red cards shown in Brazilian youth game

segments.body: A brawl during the second half led to 43 players and eight coaching staff being sent off, a reported world record. The game was paused for about 40 minutes before the referee abandoned it. Police were called after damage was reported at the stadium.

segments.title: The tie’s outcome
segments.body: Uberlandia confirmed they had conceded the semi-final’s second leg because Mamore had only seven players available after the dismissals. The club called the decision a “gesture of fair play”; Mamore will progress to the final.

content.headline: Sweeney says England must improve discipline before Australia opener
content.shortHeadline: Sweeney urges England to cut cards before Australia opener
content.standfirst: RFU chief executive Bill Sweeney says England are the world’s second-best side when they keep 15 players on the pitch, but fall well down the rankings when reduced to 14. England begin their November campaign against Australia on Sunday.

image.caption: England players Henry Pollock and Freddie Steward were shown yellow cards against Ireland.

sources.originalTitle: Sweeney demands discipline from card-happy England

segments.body: England received eight yellow cards and one red across their five Six Nations matches, and spent 118 minutes with fewer than 15 players. Sweeney said the team’s discipline had been the subject of internal discussion and that head coach Steve Borthwick was working with players to address it.

segments.title: A new tournament’s first finals weekend
segments.body: England face Australia on Sunday, followed by Japan and New Zealand, before the Nations Championship finals weekend. Sweeney said ticket sales for the new event’s Friday fixtures had been challenging, adding that some fans did not yet fully understand the format.

content.headline: Finn Russell targets historic Scotland win over New Zealand
content.shortHeadline: Russell eyes historic Scotland win over New Zealand
content.standfirst: Scotland host the All Blacks on Saturday, seeking a first win over New Zealand in 121 years. Finn Russell says he feels fresher this season and that Scotland must turn belief into results.

image.caption: Finn Russell prepares for Scotland’s Nations Championship match against New Zealand.

sources.originalTitle: No end in sight for Russell as he eyes famous All Blacks win
Scottish Rugby

segments.body: Russell, preparing for his 96th Scotland cap, says he feels good mentally and physically after finding the season following the Lions tour demanding in the past. He says Scotland need to improve how they convert opportunities in the opposition’s 22 if they are to take the next step.

segments.title: A formidable test
segments.body: Scotland have come close to beating New Zealand in recent meetings but have not ended a 121-year wait for a win. Assistant coach Pete Horne said the All Blacks had regained some of their old aura under Dave Rennie; lock Scott Cummings said Scotland had learned from past games about managing momentum.

content.headline: Everton compensation masks Burnley’s £47.8m underlying loss
content.shortHeadline: Everton payout masks Burnley’s £47.8m underlying loss
content.standfirst: Burnley reported a £9m loss for 2025-26, but without a disputed £38.8m payment from Everton the loss would have been £47.8m. An appeal over the compensation is expected to be heard in January.

image.caption: Burnley’s takeover used loans secured against club assets and other external debt.

sources.originalTitle: How landmark Everton compensation prevented Burnley record loss

segments.body: The £38.8m compensation, linked to Everton’s profit and sustainability breach and its effect on Burnley’s relegation prospects, helped make the latest accounts look healthier. The award is subject to appeal, and Burnley’s board says the outcome cannot be reasonably determined.

segments.title: Debt and repayment risks remain
segments.body: Burnley’s reported debt fell to £62.9m, but the club still faces significant repayments and is negotiating to refinance its facilities. Football finance professor Kieran Maguire said the underlying issues remained, noting the club was still losing more than £1m a week despite Premier League revenues.

content.headline: Nightclub cloakrooms now charge up to £15. What’s behind the steep rise?
content.shortHeadline: Why nightclub cloakrooms can cost up to £15
content.standfirst: Checking a coat or bag can now add a double-digit charge to a night out in Britain. Venues cite rising costs, staffing pressures and security rules, but clubbers say the price and quality of storage can be hard to justify.

image.caption: Lockers at Drumsheds in London.

sources.originalTitle: Once it was a £1 hanger. Now it’s a £15 locker. Why do cloakrooms cost so much on a night out?

segments.body: A cloakroom visit that once cost a couple of pounds can now exceed £13 at some UK venues, with bag storage at Manchester’s Co-op Live reaching £15. Night Time Industries Association figures put average spending per person on a night out at £28.06 in 2026, up from £20.95 in 2020; its chief executive says rising operating costs are being passed on to customers already near an affordability limit.

segments.title: Security, staffing and the club experience
segments.body: After the 2017 Manchester Arena attack, venues changed bag policies, with some banning larger bags and directing customers to external storage. One concertgoer describes paying £10 to leave a nearly empty tote in what she felt was an insecure room; a kebab-shop owner says he charges £5 a bag and has had no losses. Some venues still offer cheaper or free cloakrooms, while a club manager sees the staffed cloakroom as part of the social life of the venue.

content.headline: Juan Atkins, techno pioneer who gave the future a human pulse, dies at 64
content.shortHeadline: Juan Atkins, techno pioneer, dies aged 64
content.standfirst: The Detroit musician helped name and shape techno, first with Cybotron and then as Model 500. His futuristic sounds drew on new technology, but his work insisted on the emotion inside it.

image.caption: Juan Atkins in 1995.

sources.originalTitle: Juan Atkins built a cybernetic future for music – but invested it with humanity
Juan Atkins, pioneer of Detroit techno sound, dies aged 64

segments.body: Juan Atkins, who died on 31 October aged 64, was the first of Detroit’s Belleville Three to buy a synthesiser and taught Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson to DJ. With Cybotron, formed with Rik Davis, he helped establish techno’s sound and gave the genre its name; as Model 500, he made foundational tracks including “No UFO’s” and “The Chase”.

perspectives.body: Atkins’s agency told Resident Advisor he was found unresponsive in a Mexico City hotel before a scheduled performance and was pronounced dead after being taken to hospital.

segments.title: A future built from Detroit
segments.body: Atkins drew on funk, electronic music and information-age ideas, while watching the decline of Detroit’s car industry at close hand. He saw technology as a tool for creative independence, not an automatic route to utopia. His music’s lasting tension was between machine precision and human feeling: he once said the beauty of Detroit was the emotion its musicians could put into synthesisers.

content.headline: Bad Brains revisit the volatile beginnings of a punk landmark
content.shortHeadline: Bad Brains revisit their explosive first recordings
content.standfirst: The band’s newly remastered 1979 studio demo captures the energy that helped reshape American punk. In a candid look back, the members also reckon with the chaos and prejudice that complicate their legacy.

image.caption: HR performs with Bad Brains at Wetlands in New York in 1999.

sources.originalTitle: ‘They said we incited riots’: explosive punks Bad Brains on drugs, self-destruction and recording from jail

segments.body: Bad Brains’ first studio recordings, made at Washington DC’s Inner Ear in 1979, have been remastered and released as Are You Ready: The First Studio Recording. The band’s fusion of breakneck punk, funk and other influences helped drive hardcore forward, and those who saw them in their prime remember performances with an unusually intense, participatory charge.

segments.title: A legacy with difficult parts
segments.body: The group’s history also includes drug use, jail, internal turmoil and homophobic incidents, including a condemned 1989 song that has continued to shadow its reputation. Band members are reluctant to revisit every episode, though Darryl Jenifer says he respects life and loves all people. With guitarist Dr Know recovering from serious illness and singer HR being treated for health conditions, the band is unlikely to perform again.

content.headline: Niagara’s Catedral Gótica trades dancefloor certainty for spectral sound
content.shortHeadline: Niagara’s Catedral Gótica finds beauty in disorientation
content.standfirst: The Lisbon trio moves beyond its earlier, disco-leaning sound into restless ambient and skeletal electronics. Pitchfork hears an album whose varied, elusive shapes are part of its enduring appeal.

sources.originalTitle: Catedral Gótica

segments.body: Niagara’s Catedral Gótica opens with an eight-minute techno pulse and a skewed piano loop, but those dancefloor signals soon recede. Across most of the album, the Lisbon trio works with muffled rhythms, glitching frequencies and lo-fi ambient textures, keeping the listener slightly off balance rather than offering a steady beat.

segments.title: A shape that keeps shifting
segments.body: The review hears the album as a broad survey of Niagara’s changing sound, from the fractured bustle of “Novo Século” to “Gaivotas”, whose watery percussion hints at the Lisbon batida scene. The calmer closing track offers a pause after the album’s unruly journey, without fully explaining it; the critic argues that withholding clear intentions is precisely what keeps the group compelling.

content.headline: June McDoom brings her family’s Jamaican mento legacy into the present
content.shortHeadline: June McDoom renews Jamaican mento on Follow the Light
content.standfirst: The singer’s debut draws on her grandfather’s mento music and her own love of folk, then reshapes both with dub’s echo and electronic depth. Pitchfork finds a graceful record concerned with inheritance as well as sound.

sources.originalTitle: Follow the Light

segments.body: June McDoom’s debut Follow the Light reconnects with mento, a Jamaican style whose banjos, guitars and hand percussion once accompanied everyday storytelling but has since become marginal in Caribbean popular music. McDoom grew up hearing her grandfather Colin Smith play; she combines that family inheritance with the folk music she discovered for herself.

segments.title: Tradition in motion
segments.body: Rather than treating mento as a historical artefact, McDoom brings it into arrangements shaped by dub: spring reverb, deep bass and synthesised textures sit alongside guitar, strings and flute. On “Grandpa”, a voice note from her grandfather becomes part of the song; in “Memory”, she considers what she carries forward. The review praises the album’s direct writing and the ease with which it joins its different traditions.

content.headline: Dis Fig turns whispers, strings and distortion into a harrowing whole
content.shortHeadline: Dis Fig’s new album moves from whispers to sonic extremes
content.standfirst: On What to Make of These Mortal Hands, Felicia Chen builds from intimate acoustic passages into punishing noise. The review finds the contrasts—not just the climaxes—give the experimental record its emotional force.

sources.originalTitle: What to Make of These Mortal Hands

segments.body: Felicia Chen, who records as Dis Fig, has made an album of sharp contrasts: quiet vocals and pensive guitar can give way to shrieks, bass and distortion. “A Hundred Hands” begins with a descending guitar figure, while “Ginko’s Way” draws on choral harmonies and reverberation to create a stark, almost sheltered atmosphere.

segments.title: The spaces between extremes
segments.body: Many tracks build patiently, but the review’s most striking moments come in the transitions, as strings, electronic buzz and Chen’s voice change each other’s shape. The music’s force comes not only from its loudest passages but from timbre, silence and the uneasy movement between tenderness and cathartic excess.

content.headline: Two Shell’s Infinite Now tests the limits of provocation and AI
content.shortHeadline: Two Shell’s Infinite Now: when the provocation outlives the music
content.standfirst: Pitchfork’s sharply negative review argues that the duo’s new club-pop album has lost the volatile energy that once made its tricks exciting. Its criticism of possible AI involvement remains an interpretation, not proof of how these tracks were made.

sources.originalTitle: Infinite Now

segments.body: Pitchfork hears Infinite Now as a letdown: its opening track has a plasticky finish, and the album’s builds and drops rarely create the tension that would make them land. The review contrasts the record with earlier Two Shell tracks that used filters and shifting volume to make dance music feel unstable and alive.

segments.title: What the AI debate does—and doesn’t—show
segments.body: The duo has said it has used AI-powered tools for several years and defended them as instruments. The reviewer argues that the album’s sound and the 55-track bonus collection deepen suspicions about generative AI, while acknowledging that what the group used on these tracks remains unconfirmed. The wider complaint is that the music feels indifferent, whatever the production process.

content.headline: Amy Winehouse’s Back to Black gets a 20th-anniversary reissue
content.shortHeadline: Back to Black at 20: what the new Amy Winehouse set adds
content.standfirst: A new multi-disc edition brings together demos, B-sides and a live Amsterdam show, but offers only a handful of unheard tracks. Pitchfork revisits the album’s startling blend of personal songwriting, old-school soul and pop artifice.

image.caption: Amy Winehouse, whose album Back to Black is marked by a 20th-anniversary edition.

sources.originalTitle: Back to Black (20th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: The expanded Back to Black includes early versions of “Me & Mr Jones” and “Tears Dry on Their Own”, B-sides and a 2007 Amsterdam performance, alongside five previously unheard tracks. The review says the demos reveal how Winehouse’s material shifted from the neo-soul sound of Frank towards the retro 1960s palette shaped by producer Mark Ronson and Salaam Remi.

segments.title: A record, and the hunger around it
segments.body: The review celebrates Winehouse’s command of voice and reference, and the way the album makes a very specific breakup story resonate beyond itself. It also questions the appetite for more material from a singer whose brief career was accompanied by relentless public scrutiny. The new set gathers useful pieces, but its limited new material cannot fill the absence left by the unfinished follow-up recordings, which were destroyed.

content.headline: Ramayana: Rise of a Legend makes an expansive, rousing screen epic
content.shortHeadline: Ramayana: Rise of a Legend turns myth into a grand epic
content.standfirst: Nitesh Tiwari’s three-hour retelling of Rama’s exile and coming war with Ravana is only the first half of a larger story. The Guardian finds it an engaging spectacle, with sunset landscapes and an appetite for old-fashioned adventure.

image.caption: Ranbir Kapoor as Rama in Ramayana: Rise of a Legend.

sources.originalTitle: Ramayana: Rise of a Legend review – India’s most expensive film ever becomes spectacular, huge-scale epic

segments.body: Ranbir Kapoor plays Rama, an avatar of Vishnu whose exile with Sita and his brother Lakshmana sets him on a path towards war with Ravana, played by Yash. This first three-hour instalment of Nitesh Tiwari’s adaptation of the Ramayana builds its drama from the royal succession dispute in Ayodhya to the looming conflict over Rama’s abducted wife.

segments.title: Epic scale, direct storytelling
segments.body: The review praises the film’s sunset landscapes and broad, unselfconscious storytelling, comparing its adventure to The Lord of the Rings and classic sword-and-sandal cinema. Hans Zimmer and AR Rahman provide the music. The Guardian finds the first part highly enjoyable, while noting that the story is not yet complete.

content.headline: Crawlers turns a Los Angeles apartment block into spider-horror territory
content.shortHeadline: Crawlers gives its killer spiders an anticapitalist target
content.standfirst: This creature feature traps tenants in a building owned by a predatory landlord, pairing familiar spider scares with a swipe at finance bros and online influencers. The Guardian finds its comic touches and creeping menace more effective than its conventional setup.

image.caption: A scene from the spider horror film Crawlers.

sources.originalTitle: Crawlers review – killer-spiders movie offers giant-arachnid action alongside anticapitalist commentary

segments.body: A spider outbreak takes hold in a Los Angeles apartment building, where tenants already face a landlord who complains about rules limiting his ability to exploit them. The film follows Serena, an aspiring musician and building supervisor, after an exotic spider grows to enormous size and a larger, apparently semi-sentient queen emerges.

segments.title: Scares with a sharp edge
segments.body: The review likes the film’s teasing use of point-of-view, including a glimpse from inside a bag of crisps, and finds some of its jokes genuinely funny. Its targets include influencers and people in finance, whose self-importance becomes part of the film’s comic logic. The structure remains familiar, but the mix of anticipation, humour and modern social satire gives the creature feature its appeal.

content.headline: Merry Christmas Aubrey Flint gets a lift from its veteran cast
content.shortHeadline: Merry Christmas Aubrey Flint: a familiar festive tale, enlivened
content.standfirst: John Bradley’s grumbling York history buff is drawn into a retirement community’s production of A Christmas Carol. The Guardian finds the story formulaic but warmed by a playful ensemble including Richard E Grant, Celia Imrie and Nigel Planer.

image.caption: The cast of Merry Christmas Aubrey Flint, including Richard E Grant and Celia Imrie.

sources.originalTitle: Merry Christmas Aubrey Flint review – Dickensian festive Britpic decorated by selection box of familiar faces

segments.body: Aubrey Flint, a history-minded Christmas sceptic, is nudged towards a retirement community whose residents are staging A Christmas Carol. The film’s route to redemption is familiar, but the Guardian says it improves after an opening that resembles a low-budget festive advert.

segments.title: The pleasure is in the players
segments.body: The review credits casting director Lucy Amos and an experienced ensemble with bringing life to the material. Richard E Grant, Celia Imrie, Kiell Smith-Bynoe, Nigel Planer and others make the residents’ amateur production feel lively; Jim Broadbent’s narration and Imrie’s Scrooge audition are particular highlights. The film’s strongest scenes, the critic suggests, show how performers can rescue a modest formula.

content.headline: Judi Dench’s Bond memoir reveals Daniel Craig wanted M killed
content.shortHeadline: Daniel Craig reportedly wanted Judi Dench’s M killed off
content.standfirst: Dench says in her memoir that she was told Craig had proposed killing her character in Skyfall, adding to the actor’s record of pushing Bond towards a definitive end. The Guardian’s playful column asks how the next 007 can raise the stakes.

image.caption: Daniel Craig as James Bond with Judi Dench as M in Skyfall.

sources.originalTitle: Judi Dench says Daniel Craig ordered her death. James Bond just got a lot scarier

segments.body: Judi Dench writes that producers Barbara Broccoli, Michael G Wilson and director Sam Mendes told her M would be killed off in Skyfall. She says the press wrongly reported that she cried at the news, and adds that she was told the idea had come from Daniel Craig. The Guardian connects the revelation to Craig’s own request to kill off Bond at the end of his run.

segments.title: A legacy with a high bar
segments.body: The column treats Craig’s readiness to end the lives of both 007 and M as an iconoclastic break with Bond tradition, but also as a difficult precedent for the next actor. Its comic speculation about what could top Dench’s exit is a way of asking how the franchise can move forward without relying on another escalation in shock.

content.headline: Amazing Grace review: a helpline counsellor tries to reach a man in crisis
content.shortHeadline: Amazing Grace puts a helpline call at the heart of its drama
content.standfirst: Hannah Walters plays a counsellor trying to help an isolated caller whose distress is entangled with violence and trauma. The Guardian values the film’s humane intent, while finding its repeated conversations and explanatory flashbacks limiting.

image.caption: Hannah Walters in Amazing Grace.

sources.originalTitle: Amazing Grace review – blazing Hannah Walters struggles to save a lonely caller at the end of his tether

segments.body: During a night shift on a helpline, Grace receives repeated calls from Walter, a lonely man contemplating suicide. He hangs up when questions become painful, then calls again, gradually speaking about the experiences behind his distress. The film’s focus is intimate and confined, centred on the effort to establish trust and offer help.

segments.title: Sincerity and its limits
segments.body: The Guardian says the film’s evident wish to show people in pain that help exists is affecting, and praises the detailed design of Walter’s home as a portrait of his life. But the critic finds the cycle of confession and reaction repetitive, with heightened acting and explanatory flashbacks weakening the drama. Amazing Grace opens in UK cinemas on 6 November.

content.headline: Peter Medak, director of The Changeling and The Krays, dies aged 88
content.shortHeadline: Peter Medak, director of The Changeling, dies aged 88
content.standfirst: The British-Hungarian filmmaker moved between horror, comedy, crime films and television. His patient ghost story The Changeling won admirers including Martin Scorsese and Guillermo del Toro.

image.caption: Peter O’Toole and co-stars in Peter Medak’s The Ruling Class.

sources.originalTitle: Peter Medak obituary

segments.body: Peter Medak, who has died aged 88, directed The Changeling, the 1980 ghost story praised by Martin Scorsese as a film of sadness and dread and called a masterpiece by Guillermo del Toro. Its slow, atmospheric scares established a contrast with the range of work that followed, including the satire The Ruling Class and the British crime drama The Krays.

segments.title: A career across genres
segments.body: Born in Budapest, Medak escaped Hungary during the 1956 revolution and built a career in British film and television. His work included Let Him Have It, comedies such as Zorro – The Gay Blade, and episodes of series including Homicide: Life on the Street, The Wire and Breaking Bad. He later made a documentary about the disastrous production of Ghost in the Noonday Sun, a film he had once called the biggest disaster of his life.

content.headline: Wicker’s perfect husband is funny, strange—and raises questions about agency
content.shortHeadline: Wicker’s fairy-tale romance plays with desire and power
content.standfirst: Olivia Colman’s fisherwoman commissions a husband made of willow, played by Alexander Skarsgård. One review relishes the film’s bawdy comedy while questioning its gender politics; its filmmakers describe a story about domestic labour and desire.

image.caption: Olivia Colman as the Fisherwoman in Wicker.

sources.originalTitle: Wicker is unhinged and sexist. I loved it
A husband made from a basket? Why women are going wild for freaky film romance Wicker

segments.body: In Wicker, Olivia Colman plays a fisherwoman who pays a basketmaker, played by Peter Dinklage, to make her a husband from willow. Alexander Skarsgård’s creation is handsome, attentive and quickly unsettles a village built around unequal expectations of marriage. The i Paper calls the result a bawdy, frequently funny fairy tale, but questions how little agency the husband appears to have.

perspectives.body: Co-writer Eleanor Wilson says the story grew into a conversation about domestic labour and the mental load, while the filmmakers were drawn to a heroine who does not fit her community’s standards of beauty or behaviour.

segments.title: A fantasy with a sharp edge
segments.body: The review argues that the film’s pleasure in a man devoted to a woman’s needs sits uneasily beside the idea that his life is his own. It sees the imbalance as an over-correction, even as Colman’s character responds with relief rather than entitlement. The filmmakers, by contrast, frame her choice as part of a broader exploration of desire, dating and who gets to define a desirable partner.

content.headline: All’s Fair season two review: the legal drama leans into its absurdity
content.shortHeadline: All’s Fair is still absurd—and now a little more fun
content.standfirst: Kim Kardashian, Naomi Watts and Glenn Close return to Ryan Murphy’s divorce-lawyer drama, where scorpion balls and invisible-ink cases vie for attention. The Guardian says it is still ludicrous, but may be edging towards “so bad it’s good”.

image.caption: Kim Kardashian and Naomi Watts with Sarah Paulson in All’s Fair season two.

sources.originalTitle: All’s Fair season two review – am I delirious … or is this getting good?

segments.body: Season two picks up with Kim Kardashian’s Allura back at the centre of a California divorce firm, amid plots involving a scorpion-themed party, a suspicious figure outside her glass house and a client with an unsigned prenup. The Guardian’s review finds the story barely interested in continuity, and the series still crowded with extravagant names, dialogue and situations.

segments.title: Camp, at last?
segments.body: The critic hears possible signs of self-awareness in the show’s jokes, including a nod to Kardashian’s own bar-exam attempt, and finds herself enjoying the nonsense rather than simply marvelling at it. That is a modest improvement, not a reversal: the review awards one star and says the show is only beginning to grope towards “so bad it’s good” territory.

content.headline: Stick season two sends Owen Wilson’s golf pro back on the road
content.shortHeadline: Stick season two gives Pryce Cahill another shot
content.standfirst: Pryce Cahill leaves his protégés to find their own way and tries to revive his playing career at 55. The Guardian praises Owen Wilson’s comic warmth and the show’s mix of easygoing hangout comedy with grief and regret.

image.caption: Owen Wilson and Rhea Seehorn in Stick.

sources.originalTitle: Stick review – you really need Owen Wilson’s beautiful golf comedy in your life

segments.body: In the second season of Stick, retired golf legend Pryce Cahill sets his sights on a comeback and the US Open, while teenager Santi begins to pull away from his mentor’s advice. The change leaves Pryce back on the road with his friend Mitts, confronting his own stalled ambitions rather than trying to steer someone else’s.

segments.title: The feeling beneath the comedy
segments.body: The Guardian calls Stick an easygoing, companionable watch, but says its emotional weight comes from the losses and choices beneath Pryce’s midlife crisis. Owen Wilson, Marc Maron and Timothy Olyphant are praised for settling into their roles; Rhea Seehorn’s arrival as Pryce’s long-lost love adds another spark to the season.

content.headline: Tall Tales and Murder review: an Irish crime caper with too many detours
content.shortHeadline: Tall Tales and Murder is lively, but loses its way
content.standfirst: A care-home worker and a local miscreant are drawn into a gangland hunt for Celtic gold. The Guardian finds plenty of comic invention and strong performances, but says the six-part series piles up characters and plot twists without resolving its most intriguing threads.

image.caption: Ella Lily Hyland, Aidan Gillen and Casey Walsh in Tall Tales and Murder.

sources.originalTitle: Tall Tales and Murder review – this Irish version of The Wire makes for mile-a-minute TV

segments.body: Based on the first of Caimh McDonnell’s Dublin Trilogy novels, Tall Tales and Murder begins with care-home worker Bridget and local troublemaker Paul before drawing them into an underworld feud over buried Celtic gold. A dysfunctional care home, a Paul Mescal lookalike contest and a host of other diversions arrive along the way.

segments.title: More energy than focus
segments.body: The review praises Ella Lily Hyland and Casey Walsh’s chemistry, Sheila Flitton’s performance as a dementia patient and the comic menace of Philippa Dunne’s gangster. But it argues that the series’ constant supply of plots and tonal shifts leaves its central story less compelling, with early mysteries and character threads dropped or unresolved.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s future is uncertain after its Disney+ partnership ends
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who faces an uncertain future off screen
content.standfirst: The BBC has ended its Disney+ collaboration, cancelled a planned Christmas special and is seeking a new partner, with no next Doctor announced. Fans and former contributors disagree about why the revival stalled, but share concern that the series should return.

image.caption: Several actors who have played the Doctor, including David Tennant, Jodie Whittaker and Ncuti Gatwa.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: The BBC has ended its partnership with Disney+ after the hoped-for global expansion of Doctor Who failed to materialise. With no Doctor currently in place, the corporation has cancelled a planned Christmas special and put future production out to tender; so far, no new funding partner has emerged. The BBC has declined to discuss the decision in detail.

segments.title: A long history of reinvention
segments.body: The article traces the show’s rise, cancellation in 1989 and successful revival in 2005, before considering arguments about its latest decline: scripts, casting, changing audiences and the scale of Disney’s investment. Lifelong fan Frank Skinner says the programme did not need billions simply to tell a good story and wants it back on screen; the reasons for the partnership’s failure remain unresolved.

content.headline: Call the Midwife’s Laura Main on a year away from Poplar
content.shortHeadline: Laura Main on caring, change and a Call the Midwife break
content.standfirst: After 15 years as Shelagh Turner, Main has not filmed this year while the series takes a break. She discusses the coming prequel, her play about Elizabeth II and helping care for her mother in Aberdeen.

image.caption: Laura Main, currently appearing in By Royal Appointment.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I wanted my Call the Midwife character to age normally – even if I didn’t want to’

segments.body: Laura Main has played Shelagh Turner in all 15 seasons of Call the Midwife, but did not film this year as the BBC drama took a break. A 16th season and a film are planned, while the Christmas schedule brings the prequel Sisters in Arms. Main says she will watch with affection, though she finds it hard not to talk about the series that has shaped most of her working life.

segments.title: Care off screen
segments.body: Main is touring in By Royal Appointment, a play about Elizabeth II, and has also spent time helping care for her 91-year-old mother. She describes support from Aberdeen council and says the hardest step for carers is often getting help in the first place. The interview also touches on ageing on screen, her choice to let Shelagh age naturally, and her uncertainty about when the announced Call the Midwife film will be made.

content.headline: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake makes a classic feel new
content.shortHeadline: Ocarina of Time remake brings a classic back to life
content.standfirst: Nintendo’s ambitious remake refreshes the landmark adventure with voiced scenes, new visuals and easier controls, while keeping its puzzles and melancholy intact. The Guardian finds a moving return that can stand alongside modern Zelda games.

image.caption: A scene from the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

sources.originalTitle: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review – a dream come true

segments.body: The remake follows the same journey through Hyrule and preserves the original puzzles, but gives its story voiced cutscenes and livelier dialogue. Link can jump freely, equipment is easier to reach and the orchestral score gives familiar scenes renewed force. The reviewer finds that these changes draw out the drama rather than replacing the game’s structure.

segments.title: Time, and what games preserve
segments.body: The new art makes Hyrule feel like detailed theatre scenery, while the review notes a change it dislikes: the warrior Sheik has lost much of his androgyny. For the critic, the remake’s lasting achievement is that it preserves the tale’s sadness about a boy whose childhood is stolen, while making the passage of time feel newly personal. The game is due on 5 November for Nintendo Switch 2.

content.headline: Alex Garland’s Elden Ring film faces a high-stakes adaptation test
content.shortHeadline: Can the Elden Ring film make its vast world matter?
content.standfirst: The game’s huge following, George RR Martin’s mythology and a reported budget near $200m raise expectations for Alex Garland’s film. The Guardian argues that world-building alone will not be enough to make audiences care.

image.caption: The fantasy world of Elden Ring, being adapted for film by Alex Garland.

sources.originalTitle: Alex Garland’s Elden Ring adaptation is on course to be Hollywood’s goriest ever fantasy movie

segments.body: Alex Garland’s adaptation of Elden Ring has reportedly finished shooting and is in post-production, with Cailee Spaeny, Ben Whishaw, Nick Offerman and others in the cast. The game has sold more than 30 million copies, and a reported budget close to $200m makes the project an unusually expensive test of whether its vast fantasy world can work on screen.

segments.title: A world is not a story
segments.body: The article sets the project against earlier fantasy adaptations that struggled to balance world-building with a compelling narrative. Elden Ring’s creatures and bleak setting lean towards horror, but the game’s battles alone cannot carry a film. The Guardian speculates that Garland could draw on the mythology behind the game, while noting that his willingness to deny easy reassurance may be tested by the scale of the investment.

content.headline: Games presenter Dominik Diamond becomes the voice of an indie horror hero
content.shortHeadline: Dominik Diamond stars in indie horror game Draga’s Wake
content.standfirst: After five decades playing games, the former GamesMaster presenter is voicing the lead in Black Tides: Draga’s Wake. He describes learning to perform for a game made by an international team in their spare time—and sharing the surprise with his children.

image.caption: Draga, the protagonist voiced by Dominik Diamond in Black Tides: Draga’s Wake.

sources.originalTitle: After 50 years of playing video games, I’m finally starring in one

segments.body: Dominik Diamond was invited to voice Draga, a tough sailor infected by an ancient god, in Black Tides: Draga’s Wake, a survival-horror game set aboard a decaying steamship. The former GamesMaster presenter says his first attempts sounded wrong, until he lowered his voice and trusted director Greg Strangis’s guidance. Improvised fight noises, he writes, were a stranger challenge.

segments.title: A small-team spirit
segments.body: Diamond compares the game’s distributed, spare-time development to the bedroom programming culture he remembers from the ZX Spectrum era, and values its contrast with the pressures facing large studios. The game has an announcement trailer, but its makers are still in discussions with publishers. Diamond’s favourite moment so far came when his children recognised his voice in the horror hero.

content.headline: AI is making video game mashups easier—and raising copyright questions
content.shortHeadline: AI-assisted game mashups raise new copyright questions
content.standfirst: Tools that can help decompile and combine game code have lowered the technical barrier for fan-made mashups. The Guardian’s writer tests the process and finds a shift that could challenge publishers as well as transform modding.

image.caption: A video-game mashup combining Minecraft with another game world.

sources.originalTitle: Social media is full of weird video game mashups. Where are they all coming from?

segments.body: A new wave of social-media clips shows games mashed together in improbable ways, from Skyrim in Minecraft to Mario in Halo. The Guardian traces many of them to AI-assisted coding: a task that once demanded extensive technical knowledge can now, in the writer’s test, produce a basic playable browser game in minutes, though human tweaking still matters to the best results.

segments.title: The boundary between modding and piracy
segments.body: The same tools can expose game code and make it easier to combine or run existing titles, raising questions about copyright and unauthorised access. The article points to the growing ease of emulation and argues that this could have serious consequences for publishers. Whether AI companies will be made to slow or limit the technology remains uncertain.

content.headline: Playing Modern Warfare 2 again brings a father and son closer
content.shortHeadline: A father and son reconnect through Modern Warfare 2
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s writer and his 22-year-old son return to the co-op missions they first played together when the son was five. Their failures, rediscovered tactics and shared jokes become a portrait of gaming as family memory.

image.caption: A scene from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the game shared by the writer and his son.

sources.originalTitle: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears

segments.body: A father and his 22-year-old son revisit the Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 missions they first tackled together in 2009. Back then the child was five; now they bring very different habits to the controller, with one creeping cautiously ahead and the other charging into trouble. They fail repeatedly, but find the sessions as funny as the game is difficult.

segments.title: A fleeting shared world
segments.body: By learning to work together—and finally beating missions they had never completed—the two find a new rhythm. The writer reflects on how little time adults often have for games, and on the joy of playing without treating it as another obligation. Their time in the flat is temporary: they are due to move to different parts of the world in a few months.

content.headline: Does a video-game romance count as cheating? GTA VI sparks debate
content.shortHeadline: GTA VI’s romance system prompts a debate about cheating
content.standfirst: Some social-media users argue that maintaining a relationship with a character in Grand Theft Auto VI crosses a line. The Guardian explores the insecurity behind the claim while noting that real-life boundaries vary and the game has yet to settle the argument.

image.caption: Lucia and Jason, the central couple in Grand Theft Auto VI.

sources.originalTitle: Grand Theft Auto VI: can playing a video game count as cheating on your partner?

segments.body: The first look at Grand Theft Auto VI has prompted an online argument about its protagonists Lucia and Jason, whose relationship can be strengthened through dates, messages and other interactions. Some users say that taking part in an in-game romance is a form of cheating; others reject the comparison and accuse critics of jealousy.

segments.title: Virtual affection, real concerns
segments.body: The article argues that the backlash can be understood as more than a joke: for someone who feels neglected, seeing a partner invest in a fictional relationship may sting, especially amid broader loneliness and frustration with dating. Its writer does not consider game romances infidelity, but notes that boundaries differ. The debate, the piece suggests, speaks to dissatisfaction that a game alone cannot resolve.

content.headline: Could growing medicines in orbit make better drugs? The hard part is proving it
content.shortHeadline: The promise—and challenge—of making medicines in orbit
content.standfirst: Varda Space Industries has three small spacecraft in orbit, including one growing crystals of a potential cancer drug. Researchers see promise in microgravity, but repeatable results and commercial viability remain unproven.

image.caption: Varda Space Industries spacecraft in orbit, part of its effort to test manufacturing in microgravity.

sources.originalTitle: Why pharma firms are going to Earth’s orbit in search of new cancer drugs

segments.body: Varda Space Industries has three spacecraft in orbit, each carrying experiments including a miniature laboratory growing crystals of a potential cancer drug. The company says the missions are a step towards a fleet of uncrewed factories that could return materials to Earth.

segments.title: From experiment to industry
segments.body: Microgravity may allow crystals to form with fewer disruptions from settling particles and fluid currents. That could matter for medicines, where crystal structure can affect stability and how a drug is administered. Researchers also see possible uses for semiconductors, but those benefits remain potential applications, not established commercial products.

The obstacles include cost, consistent results and rules for products made in orbit. Varda plans seven missions in 2027 and ten in 2028; researchers say frequent, repeatable experiments will be needed to show whether manufacturing in space can justify its expense.

content.headline: A real photograph of satellite trails over New Zealand prompts AI accusations
content.shortHeadline: The real satellite image mistaken for AI
content.standfirst: Astrophotographer Brendan Larsen says he combined 578 photographs into an image showing about 1,400 satellites above Mount Taranaki. Its viral reception has also focused attention on the changing night sky.

image.caption: Brendan Larsen’s composite of satellite trails over Mount Taranaki, New Zealand.

sources.originalTitle: The night-sky image so incredible the NZ man behind it has been accused of using AI

segments.body: Brendan Larsen spent two hours taking 578 eight-second photographs of the night sky above Mount Taranaki. He then spent about 40 hours layering and editing them. The resulting composite shows about 1,400 satellites and 14,000 trails criss-crossing the sky; some viewers have accused him of making it with AI.

segments.title: A sky under pressure
segments.body: Larsen says he documented his process because he expected questions about whether the picture was real. He also hopes the image will prompt debate about satellite use: he finds their presence fascinating, but worries about their growing visibility and the future of the night sky.

content.headline: Manx shearwaters can lose their bearings when their body clocks fall behind
content.shortHeadline: How jet lag can throw migrating shearwaters off course
content.standfirst: Analysis of two decades of tracking data suggests eastward journeys can leave the birds’ internal clocks out of sync with local time. Experienced adults correct course; young birds may be more vulnerable.

image.caption: A Manx shearwater at sea; the birds use the sun to help navigate.

sources.originalTitle: Migrating seabirds face a surprising problem: jet lag

segments.body: When Manx shearwaters return to their colonies after flying east across the Atlantic, their internal clocks can lag behind local time. Oxford researchers found that this mismatch can disrupt the birds’ sun-based navigation, using 20 years of tracking data.

segments.title: Experience makes a difference
segments.body: Adult birds corrected their bearings, adding only a small estimated distance to their journeys. First-time foragers may be at greater risk of drifting hundreds of miles off course because they lack the experience to reorient themselves. A researcher not involved in the study said the findings support the importance of the sun compass, while noting that the consequences of these errors remain unclear.

content.headline: A bird-flu outbreak on a Utah mink farm raises concern about mutation
content.shortHeadline: Why bird flu in mink is worrying researchers
content.standfirst: The outbreak has prompted concern that a virus adapted to birds could change in a mammal host. Experts describe possible routes to greater human risk, but the reporting does not establish that the virus has gained the ability to spread between people.

image.caption: Mink on a fur farm, the kind of mammal host raising concern in the bird-flu report.

sources.originalTitle: Bird flu is one mutation from serious risk to humans – how prepared is the UK?

segments.body: Bird flu has been circulating on a Utah mink farm since at least August, raising concern among researchers because mink are mammals with respiratory cells similar to those of humans. Experts say the setting could give the virus opportunities to change; so far, the supplied report does not describe sustained spread between people.

segments.title: A risk, not a prediction
segments.body: Researchers point to two possible concerns: mutations that make transmission to humans easier, and reassortment if mink are infected with both bird and human flu strains. Seasonal flu circulating in autumn is another factor they say deserves attention. These are risks experts are watching, not evidence that a new pandemic strain has emerged.

The report says a tailored vaccine made by standard methods could take about six months, while an mRNA approach might be faster. Experts also call for bird-flu tests to be developed and checked. The UK Health Security Agency says it has systems to detect human cases and is ready to respond if needed.

content.headline: UK plans facial recognition for immigration enforcement, including civil cases
content.shortHeadline: UK plans wider use of facial recognition in immigration checks
content.standfirst: Home Office documents describe live facial recognition at transport hubs and some public events, potentially including people who have overstayed visas. Campaigners question the expansion and the adequacy of oversight.

image.caption: A live facial recognition camera, a technology the Home Office is considering for immigration enforcement.

sources.originalTitle: UK to deploy facial recognition in biggest-ever immigration crackdown

segments.body: Home Office documents show plans to use live facial recognition for general immigration enforcement, beyond the earlier trials at Holyhead port. Potential deployments include transport hubs and specific events, and watchlists could include people liable to detention for civil immigration matters such as overstaying a visa.

segments.title: Questions about scrutiny
segments.body: The Home Office says the technology could help locate undocumented people while reducing repeated visits to homes or workplaces. Campaigners warn of a major expansion of surveillance and raise concerns about misidentification. The documents cite external oversight, but the biometrics and surveillance camera commissioner said he was not consulted and that immigration use falls outside his remit.

content.headline: Cyberattacks on refrigeration systems reach French blood stores as culprit stays
content.shortHeadline: Freezer hacks hit French blood stores; attribution remains unclear
content.standfirst: France’s blood service says contractors’ cold stores were affected, but alarms allowed staff to move products before they were compromised. The wider attacks have disrupted refrigeration across Europe, with no confirmed culprit.

image.caption: A cold-storage facility used for blood products in France.

sources.originalTitle: French blood banks hacked in latest cyber-attack on Europe
French blood supplies impacted by freezer hacks as theories swirl about culprits
UK meat industry hit by cyber-attack which targeted European supermarket freezers
If hackers can take control of a supermarket freezer, how vulnerable is other tech?

segments.body: France’s national blood service says hackers raised temperature and defrost settings at three contractor-run cold stores. Alarm systems allowed technicians to intervene; plasma and other products were moved, and the service reported no products compromised. The incident adds sensitive medical storage to a wave of attacks on refrigeration systems.

segments.title: Who was behind the attacks?
segments.body: The incidents have affected supermarkets and other businesses in several European countries, and earlier attacks spoiled food. Security firms have reported evidence of scanning and possible coordination, but disagree about what it shows. Russian-linked groups, Iranian actors, other hackers and copycats have all been raised as possibilities; no formal attribution has been made.

perspectives.body: The BBC’s account of researchers’ honeypots describes targeted probing in Europe before the latest wave, but notes that scanning could also have been automatic. The security firms cited do not agree on who was responsible.

segments.body: UK officials say outdated, internet-exposed systems can be easier to exploit and urge businesses to renew and secure equipment. Researchers have also identified more than 800 refrigeration and building-control interfaces associated with UK retailers that are accessible over the public internet, though that does not by itself mean they can be hacked.
