content.headline: Study finds some smart TVs keep sending viewing data after tracking opt-outs
content.shortHeadline: Some TVs still send viewing data after opt-outs, study finds
content.standfirst: Researchers tested 12 televisions and found that data associated with automatic content recognition continued on some devices after users opted out. Encryption meant they could not confirm the contents of all remaining traffic.

sources.originalTitle: Does opting out of TV tracking work?

segments.body: Automatic content recognition, or ACR, samples audio or video to identify what is playing and can support recommendations and targeted advertising. In a study of 12 TVs from 10 manufacturers, Northeastern University researchers found that most tested systems reduced or stopped traffic associated with ACR after an opt-out, but Samsung and Roku continued some activity and a Vizio set showed no apparent change.

segments.title: What the study could not see
segments.body: Because most traffic was encrypted, the researchers could not confirm precisely what data remained in transit or whether it was processed or retained. They also found a Vidaa OS vulnerability that exposed information from users’ TVs; the company addressed access to the server, though the researchers said messages remained unencrypted.

The researchers recommend clearer disclosure of which inputs are monitored and stronger authentication and encryption. They also suggest disconnecting a TV from the internet or using network-level blocking tools. The findings concern the tested devices and do not establish that every smart TV behaves the same way.

content.headline: Bluetooth adopts optional upgrade that raises its maximum data rate to 7.5Mbps
content.shortHeadline: Bluetooth adds optional speed boost for future devices
content.standfirst: The Bluetooth SIG has adopted High Data Throughput for Bluetooth Core 7.0, raising the maximum supported rate from 2Mbps to 7.5Mbps. The first compatible devices are expected in 2027.

sources.originalTitle: Bluetooth is getting a big boost to data transfer speeds

segments.body: The Bluetooth Special Interest Group has formally adopted High Data Throughput as an optional feature of Bluetooth Core 7.0. It raises Bluetooth Low Energy’s maximum supported bit rate from 2Mbps to 7.5Mbps. The group says the change could support higher-resolution audio and faster transfers of data between devices.

The first products supporting the feature are expected sometime in 2027. Possible uses include audio devices, smartwatches and extended-reality equipment, but the specification’s adoption does not mean existing devices will gain the upgrade.

content.headline: SpaceX taps Qualcomm to build out its Starlink Mobile 5G network
content.shortHeadline: SpaceX and Qualcomm plan a large US 5G buildout
content.standfirst: A multi-year agreement would put Qualcomm’s cellular infrastructure at tens of thousands of US sites from 2027, as SpaceX combines a terrestrial network with its direct-to-cell satellites.

sources.originalTitle: SpaceX is working with Qualcomm to build its Starlink Mobile 5G network

segments.body: SpaceX plans to use Qualcomm’s Dragonwing Cellular Infrastructure at tens of thousands of US 5G cell sites, with first deployments scheduled for 2027. The company says it will combine that ground network with its direct-to-cell satellite constellation as it seeks to make Starlink Mobile a major US carrier.

The agreement is part of SpaceX’s effort to compete with established mobile operators. Qualcomm says the work could also lay groundwork for 6G, but the reporting describes a planned buildout; it does not establish the network’s eventual reach or performance.

content.headline: Midterm votes and local measures put new obstacles in the path of US data-centre
content.shortHeadline: US voters back new limits on data-centre development
content.standfirst: The election produced local restrictions and victories for some candidates favouring pauses or tighter controls. The results show political pressure on the AI industry’s infrastructure buildout, though the reporting cautions against attributing individual races to this issue alone.

sources.originalTitle: Data centers lost the midterms

segments.body: Voters considered data-centre development in local ballot measures and campaigns across the US. By Wednesday morning, results from 33 of 45 measures were reported to restrict development, including moratoriums and bans in some communities. An Election Day poll cited by The Verge found 76% of respondents opposed data centres in their communities.

segments.title: Pressure on candidates
segments.body: Several winning candidates backed pauses, local control or requirements that developers cover energy costs. But candidates’ positions varied, and the reporting says it is difficult to draw a direct line between data-centre opposition and any individual result. The votes nevertheless show the issue has become a campaign concern, including in states with substantial planned development.

content.headline: Anthropic proposes cryptographic proofs to verify which AI model made an answer
content.shortHeadline: Anthropic explores a way to prove which AI model answered
content.standfirst: The proposed open-source FlashProve system aims to let users verify a model’s identity without revealing its private weights. The research is at an early stage, with no deployment plans announced.

sources.originalTitle: Anthropic is working on a system to prove AI models’ identity

segments.body: Anthropic researchers describe FlashProve, a system intended to attach a cryptographic proof to an AI output so users can check which model produced it. One potential use is to make it harder for a provider to substitute a different model without users knowing.

segments.title: Early research, not a product
segments.body: The approach requires AI labs to publish a fingerprint for each model. The researchers say this would not expose the model’s weights, which define its behaviour. They have released a technical specification and working code, but describe the work as intermediate research and say there are no plans to deploy it at Anthropic or elsewhere.

content.headline: AI-generated pet scams use fake photos and threats to demand reward money
content.shortHeadline: Scammers use AI pet images to extort owners
content.standfirst: People searching for missing cats say scammers sent convincing AI-generated pictures, invented stories and threats when owners resisted demands for money. Police advise meeting in person before paying a reward.

image.caption: Stephanie Young says scammers sent an AI-generated image of her missing cat Buddy.

sources.originalTitle: Scammers using AI-generated images of missing pets to demand reward money

segments.body: Several UK cat owners say people claiming to have found their missing pets sent AI-generated images and demanded money, often in gift cards. When some owners questioned the claims, they received threats to sell or kill the animals. The pets in the reported cases had not been returned.

segments.title: How to avoid being rushed
segments.body: Aston University academic Rasha Kassem says AI has made convincing fraud easier to produce and urges people not to let urgency pressure them into sending money. Report Fraud advises arranging to see a pet in person before paying. The cases described do not establish the identity of the scammers or whether the missing animals were found.

content.headline: Canva cuts or changes 1,271 roles as growth slows and AI costs rise
content.shortHeadline: Canva to cut or change 1,271 roles amid slowing growth
content.standfirst: The design platform says 22% of its workforce will be affected by job cuts, relocation or role changes. Reporting also points to higher AI costs and competition from generative tools, alongside slowing growth.

image.caption: Canva co-founder Melanie Perkins, who announced changes affecting 1,271 staff.

sources.originalTitle: Canva lays off over 1,200 people amid slowing growth
Canva announces major job cuts after 'our hardest year yet'

segments.body: Canva says 1,271 people—22% of its staff—will be affected by job cuts as it responds to slower growth. The company is merging teams, reducing specialisation and moving towards hybrid work. Its co-founder Melanie Perkins called this the company’s hardest year yet.

perspectives.body: The BBC reports that some affected workers may be asked to relocate or change roles, and that Sydney is to become the main home for more product teams. Canva’s announcement describes both job losses and changes to roles.

segments.title: AI adds pressure
segments.body: TechCrunch reports that Canva has developed its own AI models to reduce costs and reliance on outside providers, while cutting its growth forecast amid rising AI expenses. The company also faces competition from AI startups and general-purpose chatbots that can generate images and presentations.

content.headline: AI is giving some graduates greater responsibility—and leaving gaps in
content.shortHeadline: AI gives some graduates bigger roles, but may skip training
content.standfirst: Young employees describe managing AI agents and taking on work usually reserved for more experienced staff. Employers and advisers warn that AI skills alone may not replace learning the fundamentals of a profession.

image.caption: Graduate Lotte Underwood manages AI agents in her public relations role.

sources.originalTitle: Graduates are managing AI - but are they learning much else?

segments.body: Some employers are creating graduate roles focused on managing AI agents, checking outputs and finding tasks to automate. Graduates interviewed by the BBC say the work can bring earlier responsibility and a wider role, while consultancy PwC found that some entry-level jobs increasingly ask for traditionally senior skills.

segments.title: What graduates still need to learn
segments.body: The reporting also records concern that AI-heavy roles may leave gaps in professional experience. A PR graduate said she still wants the chance to pitch directly to the media; a finance employer described a programme built around learning the trade. PwC’s UK technology chief says AI literacy needs to be paired with knowledge of the sector and its clients.

content.headline: Google’s AI search activity is growing faster than the ads that fund it
content.shortHeadline: Google has yet to show how AI search will pay
content.standfirst: Search queries are rising, but growth in paid clicks slowed in the latest quarter. Google says AI is adding new searches; analysts say it remains unclear whether those searches will earn as much as traditional ones.

sources.originalTitle: Google hasn’t figured out how to make AI pay like its search engine

segments.body: Alphabet says Google searches are growing at their fastest rate in five years, but Search revenue growth slowed to 12% in the third quarter and growth in paid clicks slowed to 8%. The figures matter as the company plans to spend about $200bn this year on infrastructure, much of it to support AI.

segments.title: More searches, different economics
segments.body: Google says many AI Mode queries are additional searches and could create advertising opportunities over time. But the company says those queries currently earn less than traditional searches. Analysts say it remains unclear whether AI search will create new revenue or shift users away from more profitable searches.

Advertisers cited by The Verge report continued returns from Google search advertising, but cannot isolate the performance of AI ad placements. A working paper found lower retailer revenue per session from ChatGPT ads than from Google Search ads; it does not measure Google’s own AI ads, and differences in what users were searching for complicate comparison.

content.headline: Uber says third-party AI agents booked only four rides last quarter
content.shortHeadline: AI agents booked four Uber rides in the latest quarter
content.standfirst: Uber says third-party AI agents arranged four rides in the third quarter and about 500 food deliveries during Halloween week. The figures offer an early measure of how little platform activity is currently handled by external bots.

sources.originalTitle: Uber only fulfilled 4 rides from AI agents last quarter

segments.body: Uber disclosed that third-party AI agents arranged four rides in the third quarter of 2026. The company also recorded around 500 Uber Eats orders from agents during Halloween week, against 320 million total rides and deliveries. Uber says the figures are its first public count of such activity.

The numbers suggest that AI agents are not yet taking much business away from Uber’s own app. Chief executive Dara Khosrowshahi said the company is open to working with third-party AI providers but expects its direct services to remain attractive to customers. Uber is also developing its own AI tools for its platform.

content.headline: Google faces criticism after tying schools’ Search access to AI settings
content.shortHeadline: Google faces backlash over schools’ access to Search and AI
content.standfirst: Google says schools can control which education tools are enabled, but critics say disabling AI could also cut pupils off from Search. The dispute raises questions for schools that want conventional web search without AI features.

sources.originalTitle: Google faces backlash for plan that would turn off Search for schools that restrict AI

segments.body: Google has faced criticism after saying schools using its K–12 software will not have access to Search if they opt out of its AI tools. The company says Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Search will be off by default and can be enabled separately, but its education vice-president told the New York Times that schools opting out of AI would lose Search.

segments.title: A choice under dispute
segments.body: Politicians including Bernie Sanders, Richard Blumenthal and New York mayor Zohran Mamdani criticised the policy, with former FTC chair Lina Khan calling it anti-competitive. Educators have also raised concerns that AI summaries could discourage students from finding answers themselves. Google says it is responding to schools’ requests for more control and is working on a guided-learning tool.
